goal:
Make `slugify` in `src/slugify.js` turn Latin letters with diacritics into plain ASCII: `slugify("Crème Brûlée")` returns `"creme-brulee"` and `slugify("Łódź")` returns `"lodz"`.

This covers every Latin letter, not only those Unicode can split into a base letter and an accent: letters with a stroke and ligatures take their usual ASCII spelling (for example `ø` → `o`, `æ` → `ae`, `ß` → `ss`). Accents count whether the title writes them precomposed or as separate combining marks after the letter.

Keep everything that works today. In particular, letters of other scripts stay exactly as they are: `slugify` keeps Cyrillic, Greek, Japanese, and every other script unchanged, apart from lower case.

candidates.approach: Add a Latin-only folding stage directly inside slugify before its existing separator replacement. Match Latin letters together with their following combining marks, normalize only those matches to NFD, remove their accents, and apply a comprehensive explicit mapping for Latin letters that do not decompose, including strokes and ligatures. Leave non-Latin text outside this stage so that global normalization or accent removal cannot alter other scripts. Keep the current lowercasing, digit handling, and hyphen trimming.
candidates.firstStep: Add regression tests for the requested examples, decomposed Latin accents, nondecomposing Latin letters, and unchanged Cyrillic, Greek, Japanese, digits, and punctuation; then implement the scoped folding stage in src/slugify.js.

candidates.approach: Generate a dedicated Latin-to-ASCII lookup module from pinned Unicode data plus reviewed transliteration overrides. The generator resolves decompositions and conventional spellings ahead of time, including multi-character outputs such as ae and ss, so runtime slugification does not need Unicode normalization. A small scanner replaces mapped Latin letters and consumes their following accent marks, while passing other characters through to the existing slug pipeline. Validate coverage against the chosen Unicode version rather than maintaining only a handful of examples.
candidates.firstStep: Create a generator that enumerates Latin-script letters from pinned Unicode data and reports every letter without an ASCII mapping, requiring an explicit reviewed mapping or policy before emitting the lookup module.

candidates.approach: Use an established JavaScript transliteration dependency behind a narrowly scoped helper. Send only Latin letter-and-mark runs to the dependency, never the complete title, and retain slugify's current lowercasing and separator rules. Audit the dependency's coverage and add local overrides for missing or unsuitable Latin spellings. This trades implementation effort for dependency size and maintenance, but isolates the package's broader transliteration behavior so it cannot transliterate Cyrillic, Greek, Japanese, or other scripts.
candidates.firstStep: Evaluate available transliteration packages against a fixture set containing Latin strokes, ligatures, decomposed accents, and uncommon Latin letters; check their licensing, runtime compatibility, and mapping coverage before selecting one.

candidates.approach: Introduce an ICU-backed transliteration adapter, using a compatible native or WebAssembly implementation, and apply its Latin-to-ASCII transformation only to identified Latin letter-and-mark runs. ICU supplies the Unicode-aware transformation machinery instead of bespoke normalization and mapping code; project-specific rules can fill verified coverage gaps. Preserve the existing synchronous slugify interface and bypass the adapter entirely for non-Latin text. This is likely heavier than the task warrants, but explores a standards-oriented backend rather than an inline implementation or JavaScript mapping package.
candidates.firstStep: Prototype a synchronously usable ICU Latin-ASCII adapter in the project's supported runtimes and verify its outputs for the requested examples, nondecomposing Latin letters, and decomposed accents before considering integration.

candidates.approach: Add a Latin-only folding stage inside slugify before separator replacement. Match Latin letters with their trailing combining marks, normalize only those matches to NFD, remove their marks, and apply an explicit comprehensive mapping for nondecomposing Latin letters, including strokes and ligatures. Leave all non-Latin text outside normalization and retain existing lowercasing, digit handling, and hyphen trimming.
candidates.firstStep: Add regression tests for the requested examples, decomposed Latin accents, strokes, ligatures, and unchanged non-Latin scripts, digits, and punctuation.

candidates.approach: Use a generated, checked-in transliteration table rather than runtime normalization. Generate ASCII replacements for Latin letters from Unicode decomposition data and curated mappings for nondecomposing letters. Implement a code-point scanner that applies the table only to Latin letters and skips immediately following combining marks, while passing other characters through to the existing slug pipeline.
candidates.firstStep: Create a table-generation script that enumerates Latin letters from a pinned Unicode version and reports every letter lacking an ASCII mapping for manual review.

candidates.approach: Delegate Latin transliteration to a maintained library behind a strictly scoped adapter. Extract only Latin-letter sequences with their following combining marks, transliterate those sequences through the library, and preserve non-Latin text verbatim before the existing separator replacement. Evaluate and supplement the library's mappings rather than assuming its defaults cover every Latin letter correctly.
candidates.firstStep: Evaluate candidate libraries against a fixture containing common accents, decomposed accents, extended Latin strokes, historical ligatures, and phonetic Latin letters, and reject libraries with unaddressable gaps.

candidates.approach: Implement selective compatibility normalization with an explicit repair map. Inside a dedicated Latin-folding helper, match Latin letters and their following marks, apply NFKD only to those matches to handle compatibility ligatures and presentation forms, strip marks, and explicitly transliterate remaining Latin letters such as ł, ø, æ, and ß. Call the helper before separator replacement, without compatibility-normalizing numbers or other scripts.
candidates.firstStep: Add tests distinguishing Latin compatibility forms from protected non-Latin letters and numeric forms, then prototype the scoped NFKD helper and enumerate its unmapped Latin output.
